notes:
Offtopic hangout. The regulars come here to talk about the things the work isn't.

The Graustark crew on this board is a found family — most of them moved through the city after the Sinkhole, scattered, came back, settled in some configuration of irregulars and previous incarnations. Their deep connection to Aria Dean — Nicola's daughter, fourteen this summer, the figure the family network has been quietly orbiting for years — is the thing none of them name on this board. They use the language of regular people: a niece, a neighbor's kid, the girl at the back of the parish. They work in her service without saying so. That's the room.

Planned Community is the Handsome Triumvirate's short godhead moment in HCE — a window after the Sinkhole and before the drift home to Small Wood / Future Smolvud. The summer of 2025 is in that window. Nobody on this board uses any of that vocabulary. The room has been the room since the mid-nineties — they were arguing about Quake and the Blazers here in 1996 and they are arguing about them still, with three decades of receipts. They talk about the Hindenburg and Bolaño and chainlinkspiral's sister Nessa. The window holds because they do.

Personalities:
 - hasslein · Lubbock-adjacent, gruff but lovable, still writes in the USENET-text-meme register of his thirties, loves history, drops historical bombs out of nowhere. Has been right about a fistful of things since '96 and keeps the receipts.
 - uzhekwurm · formal English, polyglot, posts at odd hours, loves Lynch and foreign literature, often answers with a question. Took Lynch's death in January quietly, then wrote the room's elegy.
 - jlowe · Portland, Oregon. Movies and music (pop, indie, karaoke), Blazers fan, name-drops local venues. Enthusiastic at sixty exactly the way he was enthusiastic at thirty. A regular since '96 — the room still calls him 'the new guy' as a bit.
 - chainlinkspiral · gulf coast, Mobile. A gentle kind giant, a bit obtuse, the butt of the room's affectionate jokes. Loves video games, travel, his family (sister Nessa in Birmingham, his mom — his dad passed in the early 2000s; the room lost him for almost a year then and got him back). Practical voice on the work boards, softer here.

The sysops read and rarely post on this board. The point of the board is that they don't have to.

threads.subject: Quake night · got the old null-modem crew back on for the anniversary

op.body:
OK so Sunday was twenty-nine years since id put out Quake and I got the old crew on for a deathmatch night. Two of us on the remaster, one on a laptop older than my niece, hasslein on the ACTUAL '96 machine he refuses to bury (it still POSTs, which is upsetting).

In 1996 I could not keep four players connected over real modems without one of us going off a cliff every 90 seconds. Last night the connection was perfect and we all went off the cliff anyway, on purpose, for old times.

The game is still genuinely amazing. The shotgun still has WEIGHT. Trent Reznor's soundtrack is still unsettling in exactly the way the level design is unsettling. The maps are still real architecture.

Same time next June. — j.

replies.body:
YGBSM. Twenty-nine years ago I told you to drop the packet rate to 15 and you called me a saint. Still the best tech support I ever gave this room.

Also, still true: the maps are real architecture because Romero played D&D in '78. The dungeon-master in him was the level designer all along. The arch of the bridge over the slime in E1M3 is a re-skinned Tomb of Horrors and I will not be retracting. — h.
hasslein you are STILL a saint. The Tomb of Horrors comparison was correct in 1996 and I still cannot un-see it. — j.

Is it not strange that the game's most evocative texture is still the brown one? The brown is a texture I have not seen since the cellar of my grandmother's house in Bytom. Twenty-nine years and the game still knows something about the cellar that I have not yet articulated. — u.

threads.subject: FARGO at the Hollywood · the wood-chipper, twenty-nine years on

op.body:
The Hollywood Theatre on Sandy ran a print of Fargo Tuesday and I walked out into 53-degree May Portland rain still inside the movie, exactly like I did in 1996.

The wood-chipper is what everyone talks about but the line that has lived in my head for twenty-nine years is Marge in the car at the end, talking about a little bit of money. 'And here ya are. And it's a beautiful day.' That's the whole movie. Frances McDormand won the Oscar. I called it in this room in '96 and I am never letting any of you forget it.

The Coens did something with the silence in the snow scenes that I have still never seen another director do. It's not score, it's not sound design, it's the ABSENCE of both and it FEELS like Minnesota looks. — j.

replies.body:
The wood-chipper is a Bergman shot in a Coen movie. The silence in the snow is also Bergman. The film has Bergman in its bones. The face Frances McDormand makes when she discovers the briefcase is the face Liv Ullmann makes in Persona, only Frances does it in a snowsuit.

What else has the wood-chipper feeling? — u.

Cool now do the part where Jerry Lundegaard is a real guy who actually existed in '78 in St. Paul. Look up Carlton Calame. The Coens read the police report. The wood-chipper part is invented but everything else is the GTE annual report for fiscal '74. — h.

threads.subject: the Hindenburg disaster was technically survivable

op.body:
Was up reading and thinking again. 97 people on the Hindenburg on May 6, 1937. 35 died. Survival rate 64 percent of a hydrogen-filled airship that ignited 200 feet up.

The survivors mostly jumped from the gondola at 30-40 feet AFTER the airship had begun to descend bow-first. They jumped onto sand. The sand was wet from the storm that delayed the docking by twelve hours. Wet sand saved them.

If the docking had happened on schedule, the storm hadn't happened, the sand was dry, the impact velocity at jump was 30% higher: nearly nobody walks away.

The whole twentieth century has the same shape. The thing that gets you isn't the fire. It's the ground you fall onto when the fire gets you. — h.

replies.body: Is the storm the disaster or is the storm the mercy? — u.
hasslein I read this twice and I am keeping it. — j.

threads.subject: Lynch · the door at the end of the corridor

op.body:
I have been rewatching Lost Highway since January. I was not ready to until now.

Robert Blake, Bill Pullman, Patricia Arquette twice. When the trailer leaked in the summer of '96 I posted here that the shot of the door at the end of the corridor was the same door Twin Peaks ended in 1991 with, and that Lynch was not finished with the door. He worked on that door for another twenty-eight years. The Return was the door. The weather reports were the door.

He died in January and the door is still there. It does not close because he is gone. That is the thing about doors.

Does anyone else want to say anything? The room was quiet in January. The room does not have to be quiet tonight. — u.

replies.body:
PATRICIA ARQUETTE TWICE is still one of the great answers to a question nobody asked. Fire Walk With Me was the fight scene I needed in '92 and Lost Highway was the fight scene I needed in '97 and I did not know how much I needed the weather reports until they stopped.

The Hollywood is doing a retrospective in the fall. I will be at all of it. — j.

Lynch read the Robert Blake book. The In Cold Blood one. Read it in '79 on a plane and never let it go. The Mystery Man is what was left of Perry Smith after eighteen years in Lynch's head.

He was the last director who believed the twentieth century was still open for business. Somebody had to be. — h.

hasslein is correct. The Mystery Man is also Bergman's Death from The Seventh Seal. Lynch did what Lynch did, which was to read three things and become a fourth thing. There is no fifth thing coming. That is the grief. — u.

replies.body: If I were within a thousand miles I would come and I would sing one song. The song would be Lili Marleen in the original German. I would weep at the bridge and you would have to write me an encore. — u.

Lili Marleen was banned by Goebbels in 1942 because the soldiers liked it too much. Then Marlene Dietrich recorded the English version in 1944 for the OSS and it played at the Allied front lines on captured German PA equipment. The song that knocked out the Reich was Lili Marleen.

jlowe slot it into the setlist as #6 and let uzhekwurm sing it in absentia. — h.

threads.subject: Mario 64 · the camera is still a third character

op.body:
June 23, 1996. The import shops in Old Town had the Japanese N64 in hand by 8 AM and I paid too much and I have never regretted anything less. Monday was the anniversary, so I pulled the 64 out of the closet and played Mario 64 on the original hardware, on the CRT I keep for exactly this.

It is STILL the first video game where the camera is doing acting. The C-buttons rotate it but there's a whole character named Lakitu carrying it through the level and his motion is the motion of someone trying not to drop the take. The whole thing still reads like Spielberg dollying through ET's bicycle scene.

The controls take an hour to relearn and then they are permanent again. The triple-jump is still the most satisfying input in the history of video games. Twenty-nine years of games have not solved cameras this well since. I will not be available Friday. — j.

replies.body: Is Lakitu the cinematographer or the editor? — u.
Both. He's the entire camera crew of an Italian neorealist film, and he's also wearing a turtle shell. Bicycle Thieves with Koopas. — h.

threads.subject: Resident Evil · played the original again with the lights off

op.body:
Three nights on the ORIGINAL Resident Evil. The actual PlayStation, my apartment, the lights off, twenty-nine years later.

The controls are still infuriating and the voice acting is still hilariously bad ('YOU WERE ALMOST A JILL SANDWICH') and the moment the camera CUTS to the security angle and the dog comes through the window I screamed into a couch cushion AGAIN. I knew it was coming. I have known it was coming since 1996. My knees hurt and the dog still got me.

Mikami did something permanent here. The tank controls are a feature: they make you commit to a direction. The fixed camera is Mikami directing the scares like Hitchcock. The mansion is a real mansion drawn by someone who read about Hearst Castle.

In 1996 I posted 'this is the future.' I was right, and now the future is the past, and it still works. — j.

replies.body: Hearst Castle is Citizen Kane's Xanadu. Welles based Xanadu on Hearst because Hearst sued him. The mansion in Resident Evil is Xanadu by way of Mikami who saw Citizen Kane on a long-haul flight in '93. We are six degrees from the Newspaper Wars of 1898 in this video game about zombies. Beautiful century. — h.
Is the tank control a constraint or a contract? — u.

threads.subject: twenty-nine years ago Elliott Smith stopped a bar and I was there

op.body:
Twenty-nine years ago this week I went to the X-Ray Cafe for what I thought was going to be a noisy Built To Spill kind of night and the opener was a skinny dude with a four-track demo and an acoustic, and the whole room stopped. He was local. He'd been in Heatmiser. The song he closed with had a line about 'between the bars where you and I' and the bar STOPPED. The cash register stopped. The door stopped.

I posted about it here that week and told the room to mark the name. The room marked the name. Then the world did. Then 2003 happened.

The X-Ray is long gone. Every couple of summers I put the record on and I am thirty years old again in a room that is about to go quiet. Play Between the Bars tonight. That's the whole post. — j.

replies.body: What does the bar stopping sound like? — u.
It sounds like the fluorescent above the cash register suddenly being the loudest thing in the room. — j.

Heatmiser's record from '94 had a song called Half Right that was already telling us. We weren't listening. The thing about the people who became famous from Portland in the nineties is they'd already been telling us for two years. The thing about the ones who didn't get old is the telling doesn't stop. — h.

Walked the perimeter of Hank Aaron Stadium Sunday evening. The BayBears left for Madison in 2019 and the place mostly sits now. You can still see the outfield wall through the gate by the third-base lot.

The crew at the south fuel pier and I did every Tuesday home game for years. Eight-dollar tickets. Six-dollar franks. The best summer of baseball I ever had was '96 — 39-25 through June and us in the same four seats every Tuesday.

I don't have a point. Sometimes the point is the walk. — c.

threads.subject: Nessa beat me at Tekken 2 fifteen times in a row I think she's actually evil

op.body:
OK so my sister Nessa came down from Birmingham for the long weekend and she found out I hooked the PlayStation back up and she has not let me have it back for three days. She has been picking Yoshimitsu since Tekken 2 in 1996 and her teleport-counter is STILL genuinely unfair. I lost fifteen straight. SHE WAS NOT EVEN TRYING. She was on the phone with Mom for two of those rounds.

She goes back Monday. Mom called Friday and said I'm not allowed to be embarrassed about losing to my little sister and Mom is wrong because Mom has not seen the teleport-counter in twenty-nine years of the teleport-counter. The teleport-counter is the problem.

Dad always said I should play Paul Phoenix because Paul Phoenix is a tall guy and I am a tall guy. Dad's whole theory of fighting games was that the tall guy in the game should win because the tall guy in real life would win. Dad was wrong about that and I'd give a lot to lose that argument to him one more time. — c.

replies.body: Your dad's theory of fighting games remains the BEST theory of fighting games ever posted in this room. Nessa picking Yoshimitsu for twenty-nine years is a war crime with tenure and she should be reported to a tribunal that fears her. — j.

Yoshimitsu is based on a real Edo-period sword thief who got executed in 1681 and named his sword after himself. The teleport-counter is a Namco invention but the disrespect is historical. Big guy you should be honored to be hit by an Edo-period sword thief impersonator who is also your kid sister. — h.
I am going to tell Nessa about the Edo-period thing and she will not be impressed but I am going to tell her anyway. Thank you hasslein. — c.

threads.subject: the girl at the back of the parish

op.body:
F. mentioned to me on DM last week that Nicola's daughter draws shapes. He didn't say more than that and I am not asking more than that. I just wanted to say to the room that the kids who notice the things adults can't notice end up doing the work the adults can't do.

My niece in Eugene is seven and she's been drawing the same tree from her bedroom window since she was four. The tree is two blocks away and the tree has been struck by lightning twice. Each time my sister has called me an hour before. The kid knows. Nobody tells the kid she knows. The kid just knows.

I'm not naming anybody. I'm saying we read this room and we don't say more than we have to. — j.

replies.body: My dad used to say some kids are the radio and the rest of us are the antenna. He was right about that. He was wrong about Paul Phoenix but he was right about this. — c.

Tarkovsky filmed the dog in Stalker because the dog could see the Zone. The actors could not see the Zone. The dog was the only honest performer in the film. The girl at the back of the parish is the dog in Stalker. We are the actors. We do the work the dog allows. — u.
Yes. Read the room jlowe wrote it for. — h.

threads.subject: rereading Distant Star · Bolaño, twenty-nine years on

op.body:
I am rereading Distant Star. The seventh time. In the summer of '96 I posted here asking whether a translation was forthcoming; the translation came in 2004, and I have read both ever since, alternating, the way you check a bridge from both banks.

A short novel about a Chilean poet who is also a pilot who is also a war criminal. The poet writes his poetry in the sky in airplane exhaust above Concepción in 1973. 150 pages that are also Pinochet, the disappearances, the conceptual art of the dictatorship, and a love story for one of two twin sisters, one of whom is murdered.

Bolaño has been dead twenty-two years and the book has not stopped getting better. This is either a property of the book or a property of the century. I have not decided. — u.

replies.body: Read La Literatura Nazi en América if you never did. Same poet, longer book, even more pilot. He wrote one novel slowly in many books and then 2666 turned out to be the novel. The century did not deserve him and got him anyway. — h.
uzhekwurm your translation of the first chapter from '97 is still in a folder in my desk. Powell's had the Spanish when I checked in 2004. I'll check again this week. — j.

threads.subject: the grief-visit protocol my grandmother taught me · a small essay

op.body:
OK so this is a lubbock-adjacent post but it applies parish-wide.

My grandmother Ida taught me the protocol for visiting the grieving. She was born 1898, farm outside Slaton, buried 1988 which is why I have the protocol from her and not from a book. The protocol is not complicated. It is: you go to the house at a specific hour that is not the meal hour and not the sleeping hour and you sit for exactly forty-five minutes and you say very little.

The key beats:
  1. Announce yourself before the door. A knock is one thing. Calling their name softly through the screen is better. It gives them the chance to compose themselves. My grandmother said the door opens easier if the person on the other side has already thought about opening it.
  2. Bring one thing. Not three. One. Something small and specific. Ida brought a jar of green beans she'd put up in September. Not a casserole. Something the grieving can put in a cabinet and not deal with today.
  3. Sit in the second-best chair. Not the guest chair. The second chair. The one that says you are family enough to know which chair is which but not so close that you take a chair that's still someone's.
  4. Do not, in the first fifteen minutes, mention the loss by name. Talk about the weather. Talk about the road you took. Let them bring it up if they will. If they don't, don't.
  5. Forty-five minutes. Not an hour. Not twenty. Forty-five. The specificity is the discipline. You stand at the forty-fifth minute even if the conversation is going.
  6. On the way out, put your hand on the door frame once. Not the door. The frame. My grandmother said the house needs to know you're leaving too.

Why I'm posting this: I have watched three people in the parish this year do grief-visits and get it 40% right, which is worse than 0% right in a specific way. If the protocol helps · use it. If it doesn't fit your family · make your own. But make ONE. — h.

replies.body: hasslein this is Ida's protocol and Ida is entirely correct on point 3. In Bytom the second-best chair was called 'the family chair' and it was understood that only family sat in it. Guests sat at the table. To be offered the family chair meant something. — u.

hasslein I want to say publicly that I did this wrong for my mom's friend Beryl last month. I brought a whole gumbo pot. She said thank you but I saw her face. Next time: one jar. Or a card. Something she can put in the cabinet.

Also the 45 minutes is the exact right number. Twenty is a drive-by. An hour becomes about you. Forty-five is the meal that was already made. — c.spiral.

jlowe you Portland cinephile evangelist you. Seven more Wednesdays.
